title: Learning to decode across languages
asked: Do children learn to decode more slowly in English than in other languages that use the Roman alphabet?
did: Children in Grades 1 to 4 read pseudowords aloud in English, French, German, Dutch, Spanish, Swedish and Finnish. Pseudowords are made-up words that follow the spelling and sound patterns of their language.
found: In Grade 1, children learning the other languages read most pseudowords correctly, while English learners read only about half. By Grade 4, English learners came close to most of the others.
means: English is an outlier with deep, irregular spelling, so its children learn to decode more slowly.

title: Speed of pseudoword naming
asked: How quickly can people read pseudowords compared with real words?
did: People read pseudowords, called nonwords here, and real words aloud, and their naming times were measured.
found: Nonwords were read nearly as quickly and accurately as real words. They were only 5 to 12 percent slower than low-frequency words.
means: Decoding happens fairly naturally, automatically and implicitly in skilled reading.

title: Interactive Activation and an unclear letter
asked: How can knowing a word help a reader identify one of its letters?
did: In the Interactive Activation Network Model, blots partly hid the word WORK. The last letter's visible features fit both K and R.
found: Feedback from the word WORK raised K close to the maximum. R rose a little and then fell, and D stayed low.
means: Feedback from known words increases activation for the letters in those words, so recognition is interactive.

title: Word frequency in the English Lexicon Project
asked: Is the word frequency effect robust, and is it just a confound of length and other variables?
did: They analyzed naming and lexical decision data from the English Lexicon Project. A multiple regression covered about 3000 words read by 30 young and older adults.
found: Frequent words were named faster across a very large number of observations. Frequency still predicted faster responses with length and other variables included.
means: How often you have met a word affects how fast you read it, apart from word length.

title: Acquired phonological dyslexia
asked: What do patients with acquired phonological dyslexia find hard?
did: Two patients, M.O. and I.B., read real words of many kinds and several lists of nonwords aloud.
found: Both read real words almost perfectly, across concreteness, word class and frequency. They gave plausible nonword pronunciations far less often, and nonwords with low grapheme-to-phoneme correspondence were hardest.
means: Reading known words and decoding new forms can be damaged separately.

who: Surface dyslexia patients MP and KT
title: Acquired surface dyslexia
asked: What do patients with acquired surface dyslexia find hard?
did: Two patients read high- and low-frequency regular words, exception words and nonwords aloud.
found: Regular words and nonwords were read well. Exception words dropped, most of all at low frequency, and errors were regularizations like DEAF read as “deef”.
means: These patients fall back on decoding, which is the opposite pattern from phonological dyslexia.

title: Early complications for two routes
asked: Do surface dyslexia errors come from a purely non-lexical route, as a strict dual-route model assumes?
did: Patterson reviewed the reading errors of surface dyslexia patients.
found: The errors showed several word influences, and made-up nonword errors were rarer than expected. One patient read incense as “increase”.
means: Either the routes combine in a more complicated way, or non-lexical reading is itself more complicated.

title: The Dual Route Cascaded model
asked: Can a model with separate lexical and rule routes simulate the main reading findings?
did: They built the DRC, with an interactive lexical route and a serial, letter-by-letter Grapheme-Phoneme Rule System. To model lexical decision, they reduced letter-word inhibition and added yes and no thresholds and a deadline.
found: The DRC simulated many phenomena in visual word recognition. Its simple rules reproduced regularization errors and the slowdown for low-frequency exception words.
means: A modular dual-route model can cover many findings, but fitting some tasks needed extra assumptions.

title: A PDP model of reading
asked: Can one learned network read regular words, exception words and nonwords without separate rules?
did: They trained a simple associative network to map orthography to phonology in a single route.
found: The model captured the frequency by regularity interaction without separate processes. Its nonword accuracy, though, was not very good.
means: Rules can emerge as generalizations from many words, but the weak nonword reading left open whether the theory or the implementation failed.

title: Better phonology and semantic lesions
asked: Was the PDP model's poor nonword reading caused by its phonological representations, and can the model produce surface dyslexia?
did: They replaced Wickelfeatures with improved phonological representations. They also added a simplified semantic system and lesioned it.
found: Nonword performance improved. Lesions to semantics caused a specific impairment on exception words.
means: One interactive system can produce both sides of the reading double dissociation.

title: Noise in phonological representations
asked: How are phonological representations and nonword generalization related?
did: They manipulated the amount of noise in the model's phonological representations.
found: The model replicated findings on developmental dyslexia. The degree of phonological deficit was related to phonological dyslexia, and word recognition was relatively spared.
means: Weak phonology alone can produce phonological dyslexia, with no separate nonword mechanism.

title: Semantic dementia and exception words
asked: Is semantic ability strongly associated with exception word reading, as the triangle model predicts?
did: They compared semantic scores with low-frequency exception word reading in patients with semantic dementia. Because the condition is progressive, they also retested patients over time.
found: Poorer semantic scores went with poorer exception word reading. Most patients declined on both together, and outliers moved toward the trend on retesting.
means: The apparent dissociations look like statistical outliers, and the association supports the triangle model.

title: DRC fit to semantic dementia patients
asked: Can the DRC fit the Woollams and colleagues patient data?
did: They generated 40,000 model patients that varied in lexical route integrity and GPC rule integrity. For each real patient, they selected the model run that best fit that patient.
found: The DRC produced an excellent fit to the data.
means: The fit came from great flexibility after seeing the data, so it explains less than a fit that is predicted in advance.

title: The wug test
asked: How readily do people apply inflections to words they have never heard?
did: Children saw a drawing of a made-up creature called a WUG and then a drawing of two, and they completed the sentence.
found: Children produced WUGS, a plural form they had never heard.
means: People, including children, readily generalize inflectional patterns to new words.

title: A past-tense network
asked: Can one associative network learn regular and irregular past tenses, including U-shaped development?
did: They trained a pattern associator on Wickelfeatures, with a training set based on children's changing input. Early training was mostly frequent irregulars, and more regulars were added later. They then tested real verbs the model had not been trained on.
found: The model showed U-shaped learning, because added regulars interfered with early irregulars. It got most Wickelfeatures right on new verbs but produced a few bizarre forms like membled for mail.
means: U-shaped learning can come from changing input to one network, but the model's odd outputs needed explaining.

title: The blending criticism
asked: Why does the past-tense network produce bizarre outputs?
did: They analyzed the network's feature-only representations.
found: With features alone, the model cannot keep competing past-tense forms apart, so their features blend.
means: Hybrids like membled and toureder come from the representation, which they used to argue against the model.

title: Phonology and semantics in the past tense
asked: Can one system explain why some patients are worst on nonword past tense and others are worst on irregulars?
did: They built a model linking speech input, semantics and speech output, then impaired either phonology or semantics. They compared the results with Broca's patients and with Wernicke's, Alzheimer's and anomic patients.
found: Phonological damage hurt nonwords most, like Broca's patients. Semantic damage hurt irregulars most, like the other patient groups.
means: The past-tense dissociation can come from phonology and semantics in one system, without separate rules and words.

who: Bird, Patterson, Lambon-Ralph, McClelland and Seidenberg (2003)
title: Controlling phonology in Broca's patients
asked: Is the regular and irregular difference in Broca's patients really about rules?
did: They tested Broca's patients with regular and irregular items adequately controlled for phonology.
found: The difference between regulars and irregulars was reduced.
means: Part of the apparent rule deficit came from phonological differences between the items.

title: Semantic dementia and irregular past tense
asked: Does irregular past-tense impairment track semantic impairment?
did: They compared irregular past-tense performance with the severity of semantic deficit in semantic dementia patients.
found: The degree of impairment with irregulars correlated strongly with the severity of the semantic deficit.
means: Irregular forms depend on semantics, as the associative account predicts.

title: Past tense in SLI
asked: Is the SLI past-tense deficit specific to rules, sparing irregulars?
did: They compared an SLI group with same-age controls on regular, irregular and nonword past tense.
found: The SLI group scored low on regulars, slightly lower on irregulars, and lowest on nonwords. Controls scored much higher on all three.
means: Irregulars were not spared, so the deficit is broader than a rule deficit predicts.

title: Weakened phonology in a learning model
asked: Can a phonological weakness produce the SLI past-tense pattern?
did: A past-tense learning model was trained with a severe phonological deficit, a weaker deficit, or intact phonology.
found: Both impaired models learned every form poorly, with regulars best and nonwords worst. The intact model did much better.
means: Phonology affects the development of all forms and is especially important for nonwords, so no missing rule is needed.

title: The chips task
asked: Do speakers of relative and absolute languages code space differently in a non-linguistic task?
did: A participant saw a card on one table, waited, was rotated 180 degrees, and picked the matching card at a second table. A fancier version combined relations from two displays to make a spatial inference.
found: Dutch speakers' responses were overwhelmingly relative. Tzeltal speakers' responses were mostly absolute.
means: Nonverbal spatial memory matches the frame of reference each language prefers.

title: Blinds down, blinds up and outdoors
asked: Could the testing environment, rather than language, explain the Dutch and Tzeltal difference?
did: They gave English speakers the rotation task with the blinds down, with the blinds up and a view of the street, or outdoors.
found: With the blinds down, English speakers overwhelmingly used relative position. With the blinds up or outdoors, their relative preference was less pronounced.
means: Language differences may be confounded with testing conditions, because Tzeltal speakers were tested outside with familiar landmarks.

title: Animals in a row with more memory load
asked: Does the relative bias hold when the task is harder and its purpose less obvious?
did: They re-ran the animals in a row experiment with Dutch college students. They added a fourth animal and a longer delay, and they moved the stimulus and response tables farther apart.
found: Under these conditions, the bias toward relative framing remained.
means: The relative bias is robust to the environment when memory matters and the interest in rotation is not obvious.

title: Spatial priming of time judgments
asked: Do horizontal and vertical spatial primes affect time judgments differently for English and Mandarin speakers?
did: People saw a horizontal prime, like a black worm ahead of a white worm. Or they saw a vertical prime, like a black ball above a white ball. They then answered purely temporal earlier or later questions. Some English speakers were first trained on vertical metaphors for time.
found: English speakers were faster after horizontal primes, and Mandarin speakers were faster after vertical primes. Trained English speakers were faster after vertical primes.
means: How a language talks about time affects how its speakers think about time, and short training can shift it.

title: Direction of text
asked: Could reading direction, rather than metaphor, explain the vertical time effect?
did: They compared the writing orientations of English, Chinese and Taiwanese text and asked people to arrange items in order.
found: English speakers always arranged items left to right. Some Chinese and Taiwanese speakers used other orders, such as top to bottom.
means: Reading and writing direction is another possible source of spatial habits for time.

title: Controlling for vertical reading
asked: Does the Mandarin vertical time effect survive when vertical readers are excluded?
did: They tested English and Mandarin speakers on horizontal and vertical time mappings, excluding Chinese readers who reported reading top to bottom.
found: English speakers were faster when left was earlier but showed no vertical advantage. Mandarin speakers were faster both when left was earlier and when top was earlier.
means: Reported vertical reading cannot fully explain the Mandarin vertical effect.

title: Mirror reading and the direction of time
asked: Can brief reading experience change how people map time onto space?
did: People pressed a blue button for past events and a red button for future events, or the reverse. So the past was on the left half the time. They did this with normal text and after a few minutes of mirror reading.
found: With normal reading, and still in the first mirror-reading block, people were faster when time flowed left to right. By the second mirror-reading block, they were faster when time flowed right to left.
means: Recent reading experience shapes the mapping of time onto space.

title: Categorical perception in sign
asked: Is there categorical perception for sign language features?
did: Signers identified and discriminated steps along a phonemic hand configuration continuum and an allophonic one.
found: The phonemic continuum had a sharp boundary between stimuli 4 and 6, with a matching discrimination peak. The allophonic continuum had shallow identification and no discrimination peak.
means: Signers perceive contrastive sign features categorically, like speech sounds.

title: Perspective in signed room descriptions
asked: Do signers understand spatial descriptions better from the speaker's or the addressee's perspective?
did: Signers saw ASL descriptions of where a table sits in a room, from the speaker's perspective or the addressee's perspective.
found: Signers understood descriptions from the speaker's perspective better, despite the mental transformation this requires.
means: Using space in sign grammar involves spatial transformations during comprehension.

title: Sign, speech and tic-tac in the brain
asked: How does brain activity for sign compare with speech and with a non-language gesture system?
did: They compared deaf signers, hearing signers and hearing people watching audio-visual speech. They also compared sign comprehension with tic-tac, a gesture system for horse-racing odds.
found: Sign was left-lateralized and used classical language areas, plus visual and superior parietal areas. Sign activated the area around Wernicke's area more strongly than tic-tac.
means: Sign is processed as language in the core language network, not just as hand movement.

title: Deafness, signing and visual attention
asked: Do deafness and experience with sign change spatial attention?
did: Hearing nonsigners, deaf signers and hearing signers watched for brief changes in the brightness or speed of dots in the center or the periphery.
found: Deaf participants had an advantage when attending to the periphery. Both deaf and hearing signers showed a leftward shift in motion-perception areas.
means: Signing changes the laterality of motion processing, while deafness itself enhances peripheral attention.

who: Early and late blind Braille readers
title: Visual cortex and Braille
asked: Does reading Braille activate visual cortex, and does age of sight loss matter?
did: Brain activity was imaged while early blind and late blind participants read Braille.
found: Braille reading activated visual cortex, more extensively the earlier sight was lost. The visual word form area was more strongly activated in early blind readers.
means: Visual cortex can be recruited for reading by touch, especially after early sight loss.

title: Five days of blindfolding
asked: Can removing vision for a short time make visual cortex take part in touch?
did: Sighted adults wore blindfolds for five days while training to read Braille, and a control group trained without blindfolds. TMS was used to disrupt visual cortex during Braille reading.
found: The blindfolded group learned more quickly and began to show primary visual cortex activity for Braille. This reversed after the blindfold came off on Day 6. TMS to visual cortex disrupted reading only in the blindfolded group.
means: Removing visual input can quickly and reversibly unmask tactile responses in visual cortex.

title: Early language and later learning
asked: Does having a language early in life affect learning a language later?
did: Deaf adults with no early language were compared with deaf adults who had early spoken language on recall of complex ASL sentences. On English grammar judgments, deaf adults with no early language were compared with adults who had early ASL or an early spoken language.
found: People with no early language did much worse on both tasks. People with early signed or early spoken language did equally well.
means: Having any language early, signed or spoken, supports later language learning.

title: Semantic blocking with simultaneous displays
asked: Does semantic blocking in naming depend on seeing objects one at a time, and at what stage does it arise?
did: Participants viewed four objects at once and named them in order, in same-category or mixed blocks, while their eye movements were tracked.
found: Gaze duration showed a blocking effect after the first cycle. Speech duration and eye-speech lag showed no blocking effect.
means: The blocking effect arises at lemma selection, not at phonological encoding or articulation.

title: Gradient effects of voice onset time
asked: Is phoneme identification for word recognition thresholded or cascaded?
did: Participants heard steps along a /b/ to /p/ continuum and clicked the bear or the pear in a visual world display. Their eye movements were tracked.
found: Mouse choices formed a step-like identification function. Looks to the competitor increased the closer the sound was to the category boundary.
means: Fine phonetic detail reaches word recognition, which supports cascaded processing.
